content:
Yesterday we studied the two silver trumpets and the different sounds that were assigned to them; the call to gather, the call for the leaders, the alarm for travel, the alarm for war, and the joyful blast over the offerings. Today we begin to look at the deeper spiritual meaning behind these instruments. But before we examine the meaning of each separate sound, we must first understand the deeper significance of the two silver trumpets themselves. And the meaning begins with the metal they were made from.

Silver carries several beautiful meanings in Scripture, and one of the most striking is its connection to the Word of God. David declared in Psalm 12:6: "The words of Yahweh are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times." Think about what that picture means. Silver is placed in the fire, and as it melts, the impurities rise to the surface and are removed. Then it is refined again, and again; seven times, the number of completeness, until what remains is utterly pure. David says the words of Yahweh are exactly like that. Every promise, every commandment, every prophecy, every revelation that comes from His mouth is flawless, trustworthy, and without a single impurity. There is no corruption in it anywhere. So, when Yahweh chose silver for these trumpets, He was choosing the metal that spoke of His own pure Word.

Now we begin to see the picture more clearly. If silver represents the pure Word of Yahweh, then these two silver trumpets; the instruments through which Yahweh's voice reached the whole camp; beautifully picture the two Testaments that we hold in our hands today. The Old Testament and the New Testament. Two trumpets, two Testaments, together forming the complete testimony of Yahweh to His people. Through them He still speaks, just as He once spoke to Israel through the trumpets in the wilderness. The same voice that gathered the camp, directed the march, warned of danger, and called the nation to worship now reaches us through the pages of Scripture.

This connection between the trumpet and the voice of God runs all through the Bible. Psalm 47:5 says: "Elohim has gone up with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a trumpet." There the trumpet is tied to Yahweh's kingship, His authority, His presence. Psalm 29 speaks again and again of "the voice of Yahweh"; a voice that breaks the cedars, shakes the wilderness, divides the flames of fire, and causes the earth to tremble. It is powerful, commanding, and majestic, exactly like the trumpet blasts that Israel heard at Sinai. In fact, at Mount Sinai, when the trumpet sounded louder and louder, Moses spoke and God answered him by a voice (Exodus 19:19). The trumpet and the voice of God were joined together. The trumpet announced that Yahweh was about to speak.

This theme does not stop in the Old Testament. It carries straight into the New. The apostle John writes in Revelation 1:10: "I was in the Spirit on the LORD’s Day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet." And that voice commanded him to write in a book what he saw. Once again, the trumpet is connected with divine revelation, with the communication of Yahweh's message to His people. From Sinai to Patmos, from Moses to John, from Genesis to revelation, the trumpet is the sound of God speaking. And so, the entire Bible is, in a real sense, the voice of Yahweh sounding through silver. Within its pages are His plans, His promises, His warnings, His judgments, His mercy, and His salvation. The voice that once sounded through silver trumpets in the wilderness now sounds through the pages of Scripture. Just as the trumpets gathered Israel, directed their journey, warned them of danger, and called them to worship, so the two Testaments gather us to Christ, direct our walk, warn us against sin, and lead us into the worship of Yahweh.

But silver carries a second meaning that makes this lesson even deeper. Throughout Israel's history, silver was the metal of redemption. When the people were numbered, every person had to give a half-shekel of silver as atonement money before Yahweh (Exodus 30:11-16). When the firstborn of Israel was redeemed, they were redeemed with silver (Numbers 3:44-51). Every Israelite understood this. Silver was the redemption metal; the metal connected with ransom, atonement, and being purchased back to God. So, these trumpets were not merely made from a precious metal. They were made from the very metal that spoke of redemption itself.

When we bring the two meanings together, something beautiful appears. If the silver trumpets represent the Word of God, and silver also represents redemption, then every message that proceeds from God's Word carries within it the theme of redemption. The Word and the ransom are joined together in the very material of the instrument. The trumpet could not sound without silver; and the message of God cannot be separated from His purpose to redeem us. From Genesis to Revelation, the central message of Scripture is that Yahweh is redeeming a people for Himself. When the trumpet called the congregation to gather, it was redemption calling God's people into fellowship. When it signalled the march, it was redemption leading them toward the Promised Land. When it sounded in war, it reminded them that Yahweh would fight for His redeemed people. When it blew over the sacrifices, it proclaimed the very means by which reconciliation with God was made possible. Every blast carried a message fashioned out of redemption.

And so, whenever we hear the sound of these spiritual silver trumpets; whenever we open the Old and New Testaments; we are hearing more than commandments and teachings. We are hearing the voice of redemption calling us out of bondage, gathering us to Yahweh, leading us through the wilderness of this world, and guiding us toward the inheritance prepared for His redeemed people. The Law points to redemption. The Prophets proclaim it.

The Psalms sing of it. The Gospels reveal it through the Messiah. The Apostolic writings explain it and its glorious outcome. Every page, whether instruction, warning, prophecy, correction, or encouragement, ultimately points to Yahweh's great work of redemption through His Son.

Now there is one more detail about these trumpets that we have not yet touched; a small phrase in Numbers 10:2 that is easy to read past without noticing. The trumpets were not poured into a mould and cast into shape.

They were made of hammered silver; beaten into form by repeated blows.
Why does Yahweh tell us this? Why mention how the silver was shaped at all? If the silver is the pure Word of Yahweh, then what does the hammering mean, and what does it have to do with the men through whom that Word came to us? That is the question we will study tomorrow, and the answer reaches into our own lives.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We thank You that You are a God of order and not confusion,

who gave Your people a clear voice to gather them, move them, and guard them.

Teach us to listen carefully for Your signals and to obey without delay.

Yahweh is great and greatly to be praised; let our ears be always turned toward You.

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
